new_statements.quote: 3. La tonologie : Le système tonologique ne possède que deux tons 'simples' ; le ton haut et le ton bas. Il n'y a pas de ton moyen avec valeur tonologique. Les tons sont fixes : c.-à-d. que les syllables dans les mots ont toujours le même ton. Ce n'est que dans des cas très rares et bien déterminés qu'une syllable change de ton.
new_statements.translation: 3. Tonology: The tonological system has only two 'simple' tones: the high tone and the low tone. There is no mid tone with tonological value. The tones are fixed: i.e. the syllables in words always have the same tone. Only in very rare and well-defined cases does a syllable change tone.
new_statements.citation: De Boeck, L.-B. (1952). Grammaire du Mondunga (Lisala, Congo Belge). Mémoires de l'Institut Royal Colonial Belge, Section des Sciences Morales et Politiques, Collection in-8°, Tome XXIV, fasc. 2. Bruxelles: Institut Royal Colonial Belge. 60 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 9, Chapter I 'Phonologie', §3 'La tonologie' (PDF page 9 of the saved file; page image)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (text, 59 pages) and the page image. Printed p. 9 (running head "GRAMMAIRE DU MONDUNGA 9") ends with heading "3. La tonologie :" followed by exactly the quoted passage: "Le système tonologique ne possède que deux tons 'simples'; le ton haut et le ton bas. Il n'y a pas de ton moyen avec valeur tonologique. Les tons sont fixes : c.-à-d. que les syllables dans les mots ont toujours le même ton. Ce n'est que dans des cas très rares et bien déterminés qu'une syllable change de ton." Verbatim against the page image, including the spelling "syllables/syllable"; only the apostrophe glyphs differ. Index (PDF p. 4) confirms Ch. I Phonologie = 1. Les voyelles p. 7, 2. Les consonnes p.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ndunga is a two-tone (H/L) language with lexically fixed tone on every syllable; no word stress or accent is described or mentioned anywhere in the grammar. The independent second description (Bokula 1982, pp. 119-120) agrees: two simple tones, high and low, borne by vowels only, generally fixed, and likewise says nothing about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (no stress of any kind is mentioned).
new_statements.exceptions: Tone, not stress: rare well-defined tone changes; contour (falling, rising, 'triple') tones on final syllables arising from suffix contraction (pp. 14-16); low tone on nominal suffixes of isolated nouns in Ndunga (Bokula 1982 p. 121). De Boeck's only use of 'accent' is 'accent descendant', a falling-tone diacritic (~p. 38).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (tones of syllables within words, citation forms of nouns/verbs). The statement is a tone statement; both first-hand sources are silent on stress rather than asserting its absence. Bokula 1982 p. 119 calls his tone remarks a preliminary sketch pending a full tonological study of the Mba group.
new_statements.identity_note: De Boeck 1952 describes 'Mondunga' of Lisala (Roby-Lisala, 1950 fieldwork) = Ndunga ndun1249 (ISO ndt); Bokula 1982 describes 'ndúngá' (locally 'mondunga'/'bondunga') spoken in eight villages on the Lisala-Businga and Modzamboli roads — the same variety. No dialects are distinguished in either source.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Ch. I 'Phonologie' (pp. 7-9): 7 vowels, no nasal vowels, vowel length mostly from contraction; §3 'La tonologie' p. 9: two tones only (high, low), no phonemic mid tone, tones fixed on syllables, rare determined tone changes. Later pages describe falling/rising/'triple' tones on final syllables from suffix contraction. The word 'accent' occurs only as 'accent descendant' = falling-tone diacritic (verb infix, ~p. 38). Text layer good (ABBYY); p. 9 verified against page image.
